texto:
Target CPA, short for target cost per acquisition, is an automated bid strategy in Google Ads in which the advertiser names the average amount it is willing to pay for a conversion and the system sets bids to win as many conversions as possible at that average. It exists because the value of a click depends on how likely it is to turn into a sale, a lead or an app install, and that likelihood changes from one auction to the next. Target CPA is one of four Smart Bidding strategies, alongside Target ROAS (return on ad spend), Maximize conversions and Maximize conversion value. Microsoft Advertising and other platforms run strategies with the same name; Google's version is the industry reference.
How the bid is set
The target is an average, not a ceiling. Google's documentation states that some conversions will cost more than the target and others less, which separates Target CPA from its predecessor, which bid against a maximum.
For each eligible auction, Smart Bidding predicts the probability that a click will lead to a conversion, using historical campaign data and signals available at the moment of the search or impression: device, location, time of day, browser, language, remarketing list membership and the query itself among them. In simplified form, a 50 euro target combined with a predicted conversion rate of 4% supports a cost per click of about 2 euros. The same keyword, in a context where the prediction drops to 1%, supports about 50 cents. Google does not publish the exact formula.
In most campaigns the advertiser still pays per click. Display campaigns are the exception: since December 2018 Google has allowed advertisers there to pay for conversions instead of clicks, an option available only with Target CPA. Eligibility requires more than 100 conversions in the previous 30 days, with 90% of them occurring within seven days of a click, according to Google's help centre.
Settings and where the target lives
Target CPA runs as a standard strategy inside one campaign, or as a portfolio strategy shared across campaigns, the only form that permits bid limits. Several settings sit underneath the campaign target:
- Ad group targets refine the campaign figure. Google discourages them, but in Demand Gen they take precedence over the campaign target.
- Device adjustments change the target rather than the bid. A +40% mobile adjustment on a 10 dollar target makes the mobile target 14 dollars, and -100% excludes the device.
- Recommended targets appear when history exists. Google suggests the average CPA of the past 30 days, adjusted for conversion delay.
- Conversion actions define what is acquired. A target applied to newsletter sign-ups and one applied to paid orders buy very different traffic.
As of October 2026, the strategy is available in Search, Shopping, Display, Demand Gen, App and Performance Max campaigns. The Google Ads API carries both a TargetCpa
strategy and an optional target on MAXIMIZE_CONVERSIONS
, which is why the June 2026 relabelling asked developers to review integrations that parse strategy names.
Data requirements and the learning period
Conversion tracking is a precondition, but historical volume no longer is. "Advertisers can start using Target CPA with no conversion history," Google's help page states, a long way from the 300 conversions in 30 days required in 2007. Kristina Park, a Google product manager, said in March 2026 that the system "will learn as new conversions or conversion value comes in".
Evaluation is another matter. Google recommends judging Target CPA over the last 30 days with at least 30 conversions, compared with 50 for Target ROAS. New or changed strategies enter a calibration period shown as "Learning", explained in PPC Land's learning phase entry. Google's wording on its length varies. PPC Land and TechWyse quote the help centre as saying calibration "can take up to around 50 conversion events or 3 conversion cycles"; the version of the same page read for this article says "a few conversion cycles (1-2 typically)".
Origin and evolution
The concept predates the name. On September 24, 2007, Google's Inside AdWords blog announced Conversion Optimizer in beta: advertisers specified "a maximum CPA bid and the Conversion Optimizer does the rest", the post said. Campaigns needed 300 conversions in the previous 30 days, and Google warned that costs could exceed the bid if conversion rates fell short of predictions.
The average arrived on May 3, 2010. Google added a target CPA option to Conversion Optimizer after advertisers said they thought in terms of an average CPA rather than a maximum, according to the announcement by Emily Williams of the AdWords team. The threshold had fallen to 15 conversions in 30 days. Google reported 21% more conversions at a 14% lower CPA for users against a control group, a self-reported comparison.
Target CPA became a standalone flexible bid strategy on May 20, 2013, described by product marketing manager Andrea Cohan as the flexible version of Conversion Optimizer. On July 25, 2016, Google introduced the Smart Bidding name for its conversion-based strategies in AdWords and DoubleClick Search, stressing auction-time bidding, and added separate Target CPA goals by device. Maximize conversions, which spends the daily budget without a target, followed on May 30, 2017.
Consolidation came next. On April 20, 2021, Google announced that Target CPA would be "bundled" into Maximize conversions for Search campaigns, surviving as an optional target field. Microsoft Advertising, which had added Target CPA to Audience Ads in November 2023, took the same route from August 4, 2025, when it removed standalone Target CPA for new campaigns and converted targets into optional goals.
Google then reversed direction in labelling. From June 2026, "Maximize conversions with a Target CPA" is again shown as "Target CPA". Google called it "purely a visual change to the labels", with no change to bidding logic.
Why it matters for marketers
Target CPA turns a business constraint into a bidding instruction. An advertiser that knows a customer is worth 120 euros can set a 40 euro target and let the platform price each auction, rather than maintaining thousands of keyword bids. It became the default for lead generation, subscription and app-install advertisers, whose conversions carry roughly equal value; retailers with varied basket sizes more often use ROAS. With manual bidding, explained in PPC Land's Max CPC entry, the advertiser prices a click. Under Target CPA, it prices and defines an outcome, and the platform decides everything else.
Limitations and disputes
The first limitation is opacity. Google does not show the bid placed in each auction or the weight given to each signal, so rising costs cannot easily be traced to a model error, competition or a change in Google's logic.
The second is the definition problem. Target CPA buys whatever is counted: a lead generator that counts form fills receives cheap form fills, spam included. Long sales cycles and offline conversions arriving weeks late weaken the predictions.
The third, and most contested, concerns targets as instructions. From August 17, 2026, budget-limited campaigns using Target CPA move toward the stated target instead of beating it. Google's example is a 10 dollar target delivering at 5 dollars, which would drift toward 10. Greg Finn of Cypress North said the change came "under the guise of predictability and optimization" and predicted "we are going to see increased CPCs" (PPC Land). Ginny Marvin, Google's Ads Product Liaison, rejected the idea of a broader Smart Bidding overhaul, arguing that unconstrained campaigns already behaved this way, and wrote that "the target becomes the efficiency lever" in budget-capped campaigns. Mike Ryan of Smarter Ecommerce reported in September that cost per click rose for budget-limited campaigns. Microsoft Advertising still lets campaigns beat their targets regardless of budget status, according to the same PPC Land analysis.
The conflict is structural: Google runs the auction, operates the bidder and reports the conversions that grade it.
Not the same as
CPA as a metric is the observed cost per conversion, calculated after the fact. Target CPA is the setting that tries to steer it.
Maximum CPA, used by Conversion Optimizer from 2007, was a ceiling on each conversion. Target CPA is an average that individual conversions may exceed.
Maximize conversions spends the full budget with no cost goal. Since 2021, Target CPA has technically been Maximize conversions with a target set.
CPA pricing, common in affiliate networks, charges only per acquisition. Standard Target CPA campaigns still pay per click. Meta's cost per result goal is a comparable target on another platform, with its own delivery rules.
Recent developments
The August change dominated the year. Google announced it on June 15, 2026, and a Bid Target Adjustment Tool appeared on July 6, letting advertisers keep, lower or replace targets before August 17. The rollout covered Search, Shopping, Performance Max, Demand Gen and Travel; Display and Hotel already ran the logic, and App and Video campaigns were excluded. Google later edited its help page to say the rollout finished on August 27, 2026. As of October 2026, Target CPA remains a labelled, standalone strategy in the Google Ads interface, mechanically identical to Maximize conversions with a target, with portfolio bid strategies as the main route for sharing a target across campaigns.

Summary
Who: Google operates Target CPA in Google Ads, Search Ads 360 and Display & Video 360. Advertisers and agencies set the target and supply conversion data; Microsoft Advertising and other platforms run strategies with the same name.
What: An automated bid strategy that sets a bid in each auction to win as many conversions as possible at an average cost per acquisition chosen by the advertiser.
When: It began as Conversion Optimizer's maximum CPA in September 2007, gained its average target in May 2010, became a flexible strategy in May 2013 and a Smart Bidding strategy in July 2016. It was folded into Maximize conversions in 2021, relabelled as Target CPA in June 2026, and changed behaviour for budget-limited campaigns from August 17, 2026.
Where: Google Search, Shopping, Display, Demand Gen, App and Performance Max campaigns, with versions on Microsoft Advertising and other ad platforms.
Why: The value of a click varies by context, and a model can price that variation per auction against a cost goal the business sets. Critics argue the platform that sets the bids also runs the auction and grades the results.
